content.text: In 1896, the French physicist Henri Becquerel accidentally discovered that uranium salts emitted invisible rays that could fog photographic plates, even when the plates were wrapped in opaque paper. This discovery opened the door to an entirely new branch of physics: radioactivity. Marie Curie and Pierre Curie continued this work, discovering the radioactive elements polonium and radium. Radioactivity is a natural process that occurs in the nuclei of unstable atoms. In this lesson, we will explore what radioactivity is, the three main types of nuclear radiation, how we detect them, and how we can protect ourselves from their harmful effects.
Radioactivity (also called radioactive decay) is the process by which an
releases energy by emitting radiation. This process is:

It is impossible to predict which particular nucleus will decay next, or when any individual nucleus will decay. Each unstable nucleus has the same probability of decaying in any given time interval, regardless of what is happening around it.
The decay is not triggered by any external conditions. It cannot be speeded up or slowed down by changing temperature, pressure, chemical reactions, or any other physical conditions.

These two properties are fundamental to understanding radioactivity. No matter what you do to a radioactive substance, whether you heat it, cool it, crush it, dissolve it in acid, or put it in a vacuum, the rate at which its nuclei decay remains unchanged.

Nuclei are held together by the strong nuclear force, which acts between nucleons (protons and neutrons). However, protons also repel each other due to the electromagnetic force (since they are all positively charged). A nucleus is stable when these forces are balanced. When there are too many or too few neutrons relative to protons, or when the nucleus is simply too large, it becomes unstable and will eventually undergo radioactive decay to move towards a more stable configuration.

Key Relationship Between Ionising Ability and Penetrating Power
There is an important inverse relationship:
the more ionising a type of radiation is, the less penetrating it is

This makes physical sense. When radiation ionises atoms, it transfers energy to those atoms. The more ionising the radiation, the faster it loses its energy and the sooner it is stopped. Alpha particles are strongly ionising, so they lose their energy quickly and are stopped by just a few centimetres of air. Gamma rays are weakly ionising, so they retain their energy over much longer distances and are highly penetrating.
Since nuclear radiation is invisible, we need special instruments to detect it:
The most common detector used in schools and laboratories
A sealed tube filled with a low-pressure inert gas (usually argon)
When radiation enters the tube, it ionises the gas atoms, creating free electrons and positive ions
These ions are accelerated by a voltage across the tube, causing a brief pulse of electric current
Each pulse is counted by an electronic counter (called a ratemeter or scaler)
The count rate (counts per second or counts per minute) indicates the intensity of radiation
Can detect alpha, beta, and gamma radiation (though alpha may not penetrate the tube window in some designs; a thin mica window is needed for alpha detection)
Contains supersaturated air or alcohol vapour
When radiation passes through, it ionises air molecules along its path
Water or alcohol droplets condense on these ions, forming visible tracks (like contrails behind aircraft)
Alpha particles produce thick, straight, short tracks
Beta particles produce thin, wispy, longer tracks that may curve
Gamma rays produce very faint, scattered tracks
Radiation fogs (darkens) photographic film, just as light does
The degree of fogging indicates the amount of radiation received
Film badges are worn by workers who may be exposed to radiation (hospital staff, nuclear workers)
The badge contains different sections with filters of various materials to identify the type and energy of radiation
Badges are developed regularly (usually monthly) to monitor total exposure

Shielding for Each Type of Radiation
Different types of radiation require different shielding:
Stopped by a sheet of paper, a few centimetres of air, or the dead outer layer of skin. Alpha sources are primarily dangerous if inhaled or ingested (internal exposure).
Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium or other metals. Aluminium or Perspex sheets are commonly used for shielding.

Never completely stopped, but intensity is greatly reduced by thick lead (several centimetres) or very thick concrete (several metres). Lead is the most practical shielding material due to its high density.
Safety Precautions When Handling Radioactive Sources
The three key principles of radiation safety are
Spend as little time as possible near radioactive sources
Plan experiments in advance to reduce handling time
Keep as far away from the source as possible
Use long-handled tongs or remote-controlled equipment to handle sources
Never point a source towards yourself or others
The intensity of radiation decreases with the square of the distance (inverse square law for gamma)
Store sources in lead-lined containers when not in use
Use appropriate shielding between the source and people
Never handle sources with bare hands; always use tongs
Never eat, drink, or smoke near radioactive sources (to prevent ingestion)
Keep sources in clearly labelled, locked containers
Always point sources away from the body
Wash hands thoroughly after working with radioactive materials
Monitor exposure using film badges or dosimeters
Follow all local regulations regarding radioactive materials
Ensure adequate ventilation to prevent accumulation of radioactive gases

Explain why alpha particles have a shorter range in air than beta particles.

Alpha particles have a shorter range in air because they are much more strongly ionising than beta particles. An alpha particle has a charge of +2 and a mass of 4 atomic mass units, compared to beta's charge of -1 and negligible mass. Due to its larger charge and slower speed, an alpha particle interacts more strongly with air molecules, ionising many atoms along its path. Each ionisation event removes energy from the alpha particle. Because alpha particles lose energy so rapidly through these frequent ionisation events, they are quickly brought to a stop after only a few centimetres. Beta particles, being lighter and having less charge, ionise fewer atoms per centimetre and therefore retain their energy over a longer distance.

Some may emit visible light due to other effects (such as radium paint, which glows because of phosphorescent chemicals mixed with it, not because of the radiation itself), but radiation is invisible to the naked eye.
Being exposed to alpha, beta, or gamma radiation does not generally make an object radioactive. This is called
, and the object does not become a source of radiation itself. However, if radioactive material gets onto or into an object, that is called
, and the object will then emit radiation until the radioactive material is removed or decays. This distinction between irradiation and contamination is very important.
Misconception 3: "You can turn radioactivity on and off"

Radioactive decay is spontaneous and cannot be started, stopped, or controlled by any physical or chemical means. You cannot switch it off by cooling the material or by applying electric fields. The decay rate depends only on the type of radioactive isotope and the number of undecayed nuclei present.
Misconception 4: "Alpha radiation is harmless because it has low penetrating power"

While alpha particles cannot penetrate the skin, they are extremely dangerous if an alpha-emitting source is inhaled, swallowed, or enters the body through a wound. Inside the body, the strong ionising ability of alpha particles causes severe damage to cells and DNA. Alpha radiation is the most dangerous type when it is an internal hazard.
Misconception 5: "All radiation is artificial and dangerous"

Background radiation is a natural part of our environment. Humans have evolved with constant exposure to low levels of natural radiation. The level of background radiation we are normally exposed to is generally considered safe.

(explanation with physics reasoning) Gamma rays are more penetrating because they have no charge and no mass, so they interact very weakly with matter. They ionise very few atoms per centimetre, losing energy slowly and therefore travelling much further before being absorbed. Alpha particles have a charge of +2 and a large mass (4 u), so they interact strongly with atoms, ionising many along their path. They lose energy rapidly and are stopped after only a few centimetres of air.

Natural sources (any three): radon gas from rocks and soil; cosmic rays from space; radioactive isotopes in rocks and soil (e.g. uranium, thorium); radioactive isotopes in food and drink (e.g. potassium-40, carbon-14); internal radiation from atoms in the body. Artificial sources (any two): medical X-rays and CT scans; nuclear weapons testing fallout; nuclear power stations; industrial uses of radioactive materials.

(explanation with physics reasoning) Radiation enters the GM tube through a thin window. The radiation ionises the low-pressure gas (argon) inside the tube, knocking electrons from gas atoms to create ions and free electrons. A high voltage across the tube accelerates these ions, causing a brief pulse of current. Each pulse is registered by an electronic counter. The number of pulses per second or per minute gives the count rate.

Any three from: use long-handled tongs to hold sources (never touch with bare hands); keep sources pointed away from the body and other people; minimise time spent near sources; keep as far from the source as practicable; store sources in lead-lined containers when not in use; never eat, drink, or smoke near sources; wash hands after the experiment.

(comparison) At arm's length, the alpha source is less dangerous than a gamma source because alpha particles are stopped by a few centimetres of air and cannot reach the body. Gamma rays, however, can travel through air and penetrate the body, causing ionisation of internal cells.

If swallowed, the alpha source becomes more dangerous because alpha particles are strongly ionising (charge +2, mass 4 u). Inside the body, they are in direct contact with living cells and can cause severe damage to DNA and tissue. The high ionising ability that makes them easy to stop externally makes them extremely harmful internally.

(explanation with physics reasoning) Alpha particles are large (mass 4 u) and strongly charged (+2), so they ionise many air molecules along their path, creating a dense trail of ions visible as thick, straight tracks. They lose energy quickly, so the tracks are short. Their large momentum means they are not easily deflected, so tracks are straight.

Beta particles are much lighter (1/1836 u) and have a smaller charge (-1), so they ionise fewer air molecules per centimetre, producing thinner tracks. They travel further before losing their energy, so tracks are longer. Their small mass means they are easily deflected by collisions, so tracks appear wispy and may curve.
